vulnerabilities.details: A vulnerability in the in-band key negotiation exists in the AWS S3 Crypto SDK for GoLang versions prior to V2. An attacker with write access to the targeted bucket can change the encryption algorithm of an object in the bucket, which can then allow them to change AES-GCM to AES-CTR. Using this in combination with a decryption oracle can reveal the authentication key used by AES-GCM as decrypting the GMAC tag leaves the authentication key recoverable as an algebraic equation. It is recommended to update your SDK to V2 or later, and re-encrypt your files.
vulnerabilities.summary: In-band key negotiation issue in AWS S3 Crypto SDK for golang in github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go

credits.name: Sophie Schmieg from the Google ISE team

vulnerabilities.details: A padding oracle vulnerability exists in the AWS S3 Crypto SDK for GoLang versions prior to V2. The SDK allows users to encrypt files with AES-CBC without computing a Message Authentication Code (MAC), which then allows an attacker who has write access to the target's S3 bucket and can observe whether or not an endpoint with access to the key can decrypt a file, they can reconstruct the plaintext with (on average) 128*length (plaintext) queries to the endpoint, by exploiting CBC's ability to manipulate the bytes of the next block and PKCS5 padding errors. It is recommended to update your SDK to V2 or later, and re-encrypt your files.
vulnerabilities.summary: CBC padding oracle issue in AWS S3 Crypto SDK for golang in github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go

vulnerabilities.details: Opentelemetry-go's baggage parsing no longer caps raw header length in go.opentelemetry.io/otel
vulnerabilities.summary: Opentelemetry-go's baggage parsing no longer caps raw header length in go.opentelemetry.io/otel

vulnerabilities.details:
The golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp package is unsafe by design, has numerous known security issues, is not maintained, and should not be used.

If you are required to interoperate with OpenPGP systems and need a maintained package, consider github.com/ProtonMail/go-crypto/openpgp which is a maintained fork that aims to be a drop-in replacement for this package.
vulnerabilities.summary: The golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp package is unmaintained, unsafe by design, and has known security issues

vulnerabilities.details: VP8L decoding in golang.org/x/image/vp8l can allocate an excessive amount of memory when processing a crafted VP8L image containing many unused Huffman tree groups. This allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via memory exhaustion.
vulnerabilities.summary: Excessive memory allocation during VP8L decoding in golang.org/x/image

vulnerabilities.details: A norm.Iter can enter an infinite loop when handling input containing invalid UTF-8 bytes.
vulnerabilities.summary: Infinite loop on invalid input in golang.org/x/text

vulnerabilities.details: The Nickname profile can panic with an out-of-bounds slice error when transforming crafted input into a short destination buffer.
vulnerabilities.summary: Panic parsing crafted input in x/text/secure/precis in golang.org/x/text

vulnerabilities.details: The source-address critical option in the Permissions returned by an authentication callback was only enforced for the PublicKeyCallback and VerifiedPublicKeyCallback paths, extending the fix for CVE-2026-46595. Permissions returned by the PasswordCallback, KeyboardInteractiveCallback, NoClientAuthCallback, and GSSAPIWithMICConfig.AllowLogin callbacks were not validated against the client's remote address, so a source-address restriction set by those callbacks was silently ignored. The check is now applied to the Permissions returned by any authentication callback.
vulnerabilities.summary: Source-address critical option not enforced for non-public-key auth callbacks in golang.org/x/crypto/ssh

vulnerabilities.details:
Previously, a channel registered in the mux's chanList is not usable until it is established. A malicious peer was able flood the channel's incomingRequests, deadlocking the entire connection.

Now, we add an atomic established state, set when a channel becomes usable. Until such a time, handlePacket drops every packet other than the open confirmation/failure, without blocking and without tearing down the connection.
vulnerabilities.summary: Prevent DoS on deadlocked undecided channel in golang.org/x/crypto/ssh

vulnerabilities.details:
Previously, after a channel has been established, a malicious peer could send crafted messages that would deadlock the entire connection.

Now, we handle all RFC 4254 channel messages; global requests are handled explicitly. Then, treat all other messages as a protocol error and tear the connection down instead of buffering and blocking.
vulnerabilities.summary: Prevent DoS on deadlocked established channel in golang.org/x/crypto/ssh

vulnerabilities.details:
A malicious GOPROXY was previously capable of forging up to two sumdb tiles that allow for a requested module to bypass the GOSUMDB check and persist attacker-controlled module content to a local Go module cache.

This attack allows for a malicious GOPROXY to serve malicious module content that cannot be detected by evaluating the transparency log.

All tiles are now correctly verified against their parents.

In order to determine if you have been affected:

rm -r go.sum go.work.sum vendor/ && go mod tidy
vulnerabilities.summary: Fix transparency log tile verification bypass in golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/tlog

vulnerabilities.details:
A malicious GOSUMDB was capable of serving arbitrary module content not contained within the transparency log.

This attack allows for a coordinating GOPROXY and GOSUMDB to serve a client malicious module content that cannot be detected by evaluating the transparency log.

In order to determine if you have been affected:

rm -r go.sum go.work.sum vendor/ && go mod tidy
vulnerabilities.summary: Ignore unrelated, unauthenticated hashes in Lookup in golang.org/x/mod/sumdb

credits.name: RyotaK (https://ryotak.net) of GMO Flatt Security Inc.

vulnerabilities.details: When "Trailer" headers are sent by a client, the HTTP server internally uses the header values to populate the Request.Trailer map passed to the server handler. Because Request.Trailer is a map, each entry incurs memory overhead. For HTTP/2 servers, a malicious client can exploit this by sending a "Trailer" header that declares a large number of fields, causing the server to allocate a disproportionate amount of memory while bypassing Server.MaxHeaderValueCount and Server.MaxHeaderBytes limits. This exploit is not applicable for HTTP/1 servers, which do not support multiplexing a large number of requests over one TCP connection, and whose Server.MaxHeaderBytes are calculated differently.
vulnerabilities.summary: HTTP/2 server memory exhaustion due to Trailer headers in net/http

vulnerabilities.details: Historically, we have been rather lax about malformed framing-related headers in our HTTP/2 implementation, as they cannot interfere with HTTP/2 framing. However, this makes it possible for our HTTP/2 implementation to forward responses containing such headers to an HTTP/1 client when acting as a reverse proxy. If the HTTP/1 client also does not behave strictly enough, this can result in response smuggling.
vulnerabilities.summary: HTTP/2 transport accepts malformed framing-related headers in net/http

vulnerabilities.details: A malicious HTTP/2 peer can cause excessive CPU consumption in the client or server by opening a large number of streams and then sending many small SETTINGS frames containing SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE values.
vulnerabilities.summary: Excessive CPU consumption from repeated initial window changes in net/http

vulnerabilities.details: The HTTP/2 server can refund connection-level flow control twice for the same data: Once when a client resets a stream (refunding data for any sent-but-unread portion of the stream), and again when a request handler reads the buffered data. A malicious client can exploit this to bypass the configured connection-level flow control limit (MaxReceiveBufferPerConnection). Total buffered data is still limited by the concurrent stream limit and stream-level flow control.
vulnerabilities.summary: Double flow control refund on HTTP/2 server streams in net/http

credits.name: RyotaK (https://ryotak.net) of GMO Flatt Security Inc.

vulnerabilities.details: HTTP/2 servers could end up crashing due to inadvertently modifying its HPACK encoder concurrently. This happens because the server modifies the HPACK encoder from two goroutines without synchronization: one uses the encoder to encode a HEADERS frame as part of a response sent to a client and the other modifies the encoder's table size when handling a SETTINGS frame containing SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE that a client sends. A malicious client can repeatedly send a request while changing the header table size to crash the server.
vulnerabilities.summary: HTTP/2 server crash due to HPACK encoder race in net/http

vulnerabilities.details:
When coalescing adjacent text nodes in addText and fosterParent, appending to an existing TextNode's Data via string concatenation (n.Data += text) reallocated and copied the accumulated string on every token. Inputs containing many short text runs separated by ignored end tags (such as "a</x>") caused O(n^2) allocations and byte copies.

Accumulate coalesced text in per-node byte slices during parsing and materialize Data strings once at the end of parse.
vulnerabilities.summary: Avoid quadratic complexity when coalescing text nodes in html in golang.org/x/net

vulnerabilities.details:
In childTextNodesAreLiteral, walking up the tree previously stopped at the nearest foreign ancestor once an HTML integration point was found. However, that integration point may itself be a descendant of an element that was foster-parented into a foreign namespace (such as <mglyph> or <malignmark> fostered under <mtext>), causing a parser to resolve the subtree in a different foreign namespace upon re-parsing the rendered output.

Continue walking the full ancestor chain and verify that every transition from a non-empty namespace occurs at an HTML integration point before emitting literal text.
vulnerabilities.summary: Check all ancestor namespace transitions when rendering raw text in html in golang.org/x/net

vulnerabilities.details: The Nickname profile can panic with an out-of-bounds slice error when transforming crafted input into a short destination buffer.
vulnerabilities.summary: Panic parsing crafted input in x/text/secure/precis in golang.org/x/text

vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

Several operations intended to be constant-time could execute secret-dependent
branches, depending on the compiler and target CPU. These include subtraction,
zero counting, division, and Montgomery multiplication.

Additionally, `UintRef` equality could terminate at the first unequal limb,
and `BoxedMontyForm::invert` branched on whether an inverse exists.

## Impact

Applications using affected operations on secret integers may leak information
through timing or microarchitectural side channels. This includes information
about intermediate arithmetic values, matching limbs, and invertibility.

Such leakage could potentially enable recovery of cryptographic secrets.
Practical exploitability depends on the downstream algorithm, compiler, target
CPU, and an attacker's ability to observe the side channel.

## Resolution

Upgrade to v0.7.6, which removes the identified branches, updates `ctutils` to
include its constant-time fixes, and adds BINSEC-based regression checks using
`cargo checkct` for arithmetic on multiple targets.
vulnerabilities.summary: Multiple timing variability issues in operations intended to be constant-time

vulnerabilities.details:
The [`derivative`](https://crates.io/crates/derivative) crate is no longer maintained.
Consider using any alternative, for instance:
- [derive_more](https://crates.io/crates/derive_more)
- [derive-where](https://crates.io/crates/derive-where)
- [educe](https://crates.io/crates/educe)
vulnerabilities.summary: `derivative` is unmaintained; consider using an alternative

vulnerabilities.details: The maintainers recommend using [k256](https://crates.io/crates/k256) instead.
vulnerabilities.summary: libsecp256k1 is unmaintained

vulnerabilities.details:
The creator of the crate `paste` has stated in the [`README.md`](https://github.com/dtolnay/paste/blob/master/README.md) 
that this project is not longer maintained as well as archived the repository

## Possible Alternative(s)

- [`pastey`]: a fork of paste and is aimed to be a drop-in replacement with additional features for paste crate
- [`with_builtin_macros`]: crate providing a [superset of `paste`'s functionality including general `macro_rules!` eager expansions](https://docs.rs/with_builtin_macros/0.1.0/with_builtin_macros/macro.with_eager_expansions.html)  and `concat!`/`concat_idents!` macros

[`pastey`]: https://crates.io/crates/pastey
[`with_builtin_macros`]: https://crates.io/crates/with_builtin_macros
vulnerabilities.summary: paste - no longer maintained

vulnerabilities.details:
`tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd` provides safe constructors (`new`, `with_interest`, `try_new`, and `try_with_interest`) that accept any `T: AsRawFd` rather than requiring proof of ownership or validity of the file descriptor. Because `RawFd` implements `AsRawFd`, safe code can construct an `AsyncFd` from an arbitrary or closed file descriptor, or close/replace the underlying file descriptor while the `AsyncFd` is still alive.

This violates I/O safety in two ways:

1. `AsyncFd<T>` implements `AsFd` for all `T: AsRawFd` by calling `BorrowedFd::borrow_raw(self.as_raw_fd())`, allowing safe code to obtain an arbitrary `BorrowedFd<'_>` without owning the file descriptor.
2. Tokio's I/O driver stores a pointer to an internal allocation in the `epoll`/`kqueue` user data for registered file descriptors. If the underlying file descriptor is duplicated and then closed while an `AsyncFd` is alive, and the OS reuses that file descriptor number for a another IO resource on the same runtime, dropping the first `AsyncFd` deregisters the reused file descriptor number and frees the first while the original file description remains registered in `epoll`, leading to a use-after-free when a readiness event fires.

Starting in Tokio 1.51.6, 1.53.3, and 1.54.0, `AsyncFd::new`, `AsyncFd::with_interest`, `AsyncFd::try_new`, and `AsyncFd::try_with_interest` are deprecated in favor of the `unsafe` constructors `AsyncFd::register` and `AsyncFd::register_with_interest`. Callers must ensure that the file descriptor remains valid, open, and unchanged for the lifetime of the `AsyncFd`.
vulnerabilities.summary: `AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate I/O safety
